phonemes.desc: Voiceless pharyngeal fricative [ħ], the same dry throat-sound that opens Heka and Hu.
Long stressed vowel; the name's peak, carrying the god's height and distance.
Alveolar tap or trill [r], like a brief roll of the tongue.
Final short vowel, reconstructed from Coptic ⲟⲩⲣ (our) / ⲏⲣⲟ (hēro).

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-roo' — the first syllable is throaty and drawn out, the second light and ascending, like a falcon rising.

kin.label: Egyptian
kin.form: ḥr, 'the distant one' or 'the one on high' (Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache III, s.v. ḥr)

pronunciation.note: Horus is Tier 1 because the Egyptian Ḥr preserves the underdotted ḥ — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. The name is onomatopoeically apt: the throaty ḥ and the final u suggest a cry from far above. The Greek borrowing Hōros adds an omega, but the original Egyptian root is simply ḥr.

domains.title: The Distant One
domains.subtitle: Sky · Kingship · Falcon
domains.lead: Ḥr is the falcon of the sky, whose eyes are the sun and the moon, whose wings outspread are the heavens, and whose incarnation on earth is the living pharaoh. He is not one god but a constellation of related gods — Horus the Elder, the primordial sky; Horus the Younger, son of Osiris and Isis; and Re-Horakhty, the solar synthesis. Through all his forms he stands for one thing: legitimate authority defending cosmic order against chaos.

cards.name: The Sky
cards.desc: Horus soars across the heavens; his right eye is the sun, his left the moon, and his body the luminous air.

cards.name: Divine Kingship
cards.desc: Every pharaoh is the 'Living Horus'; the Horus-name is the first and oldest of the five royal names.

cards.name: The Falcon
cards.desc: The lanner or peregrine falcon — swift, far-seeing, and deadly — is Horus's living embodiment.

cards.name: The Wedjat Eye
cards.desc: The restored eye of Horus is Egypt's supreme symbol of protection, wholeness, and royal health.

mythology.lead: Horus's mythology is the political theology of Egypt made personal. It tells how the rightful heir, born from a murdered father and a resourceful mother, defeats the usurper and restores the throne. The story was never merely entertainment; it was the charter of kingship, replayed in temples for three thousand years.

myths.title: Elder and Younger
myths.text: Two falcons answer to the name Ḥr, and the Egyptians rarely troubled to separate them. Horus the Elder (Ḥr-wr) is the primordial sky of the Pyramid Texts, brother of Osiris and Set, whose eyes are the sun and the moon — when he weeps, the Nile rises. Horus the Younger (Ḥr-pꜣ-ꜥd, 'Horus the child') is the son of Osiris and Isis, avenger of his father. By the New Kingdom the two had merged into a single royal figure: the Horus of Edfu is at once the ancient sky and the young heir. The fusion was not confusion but policy — the king's god had to be older than creation yet younger than his own succession. The myth means that legitimacy in Egypt drew on two wells, antiquity and inheritance, and Horus drew from both.

myths.title: Eighty Years Against Set
myths.text: When Set murders Osiris and seizes the throne, the infant Horus is hidden in the Delta marshes of Chemmis, guarded by Isis and the scorpion Serqet. Grown to manhood, he claims his inheritance, and the dispute goes before the Ennead. The New Kingdom satire The Contendings of Horus and Set (Papyrus Chester Beatty I) turns the cosmic lawsuit into eighty years of grotesque trials: the hippopotamus duel in the river's depths, the shameful episode of the lettuce, Isis disguised as a maiden tricking Set into judging against himself, and the tribunal's own judges oscillating 'like lunatics.' Set tears out Horus's eyes; at last the verdict favours legitimacy over force, and the gods divide the inheritance — Horus the black land, Set the desert. Plutarch retells the whole contest in Greek (De Iside 19–20), already calling it ancient. The myth is Egypt's constitution in narrative form: the crown follows the bloodline of Osiris, and chaos must settle for the frontier.

myths.title: The Wedjat
myths.text: Set's violence costs Horus his eye — the Pyramid Texts already know the motif (Utterance 478: Horus recovers the wedjat-eye from Set). The eye is buried and sprouts lotuses; Ḏḥwtj heals it, or the goddess Hathor restores it with gazelle's milk, and it becomes the wedjat, 'the whole one.' Later tradition mapped the eye's six parts onto the fractions 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, and 1/64 — summing to 63/64, the missing sixty-fourth supplied by Thoth's magic, an emblem of the ineradicable remainder that only speech completes. From the gods the restored eye passes to the dead: painted on mummies and worn as amulets from the Middle Kingdom onward, it is Egypt's supreme sign of protection. The myth teaches that what violence breaks, order can make whole again — and that wholeness, not victory, is the true spoil of the war with chaos.

myths.title: The Living Horus
myths.text: From the Narmer Palette onward the falcon stands behind the king's head, and the serekh — the palace-façade frame holding the Horus-name — is the oldest element of the royal titulary, older than the cartouche. The theology is a relay: the dead pharaoh becomes Osiris, his successor becomes the new Horus, and every coronation re-runs the original victory over Set (Pyramid Texts, Utterance 570, already address the king as 'this Horus'). In life the king is 'the Living Horus,' son of Isis and Osiris by adoption into the divine household. At Edfu, the best-preserved temple in Egypt, the walls still stage the drama annually: the 'Triumph of Horus' over Set and his followers, complete with sacred barque and a hippopotamus of wax. The myth converts politics into cosmology: every reign is the restoration of order, and every usurper a reincarnation of the desert.

myths.title: Behdety Burns the Rebels
myths.text: The temple of Edfu preserves a myth found nowhere else in this form: Horus of Edfu — Behdety, 'He of the winged disk' — takes the form of the sun's winged disk to hunt the followers of Set who hide in the northern marshes. From the sky he burns them with fire; Set himself is speared and bound, his allies dismembered among the rushes. The king's earthly enemies are written into the drama as the god's enemies, so that every victory of Horus at Edfu is simultaneously a victory of pharaoh. The myth's afterlife is iconographic: from the New Kingdom to the Roman period the winged sun-disk flies above temple gates across Egypt and beyond — an airborne talisman of royal power that sees everywhere and strikes from above. It is the falcon's-eye view of kingship made permanent over every doorway: the sky-god's body become a sign of passage and protection.

lore.syncretism: Horus absorbed and was absorbed by many gods. As Re-Horakhty he united the falcon with the solar disk; as Harpocrates he became the finger-to-lips divine child of Greco-Roman Egypt; as Sokar and Montu he shared falcon imagery with other deities of death and war. Plutarch's De Iside et Osiride transmitted the Osiris-Horus myth to the Greek and Roman world, where it influenced conceptions of divine sonship and resurrection. Some later interpreters, from early Christians to modern comparative mythologists, have drawn parallels between Horus and other divine-child figures, though many of these claims are exaggerated or unsupported by Egyptian evidence.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Eye of Horus is arguably the most widely recognised symbol of ancient Egypt. It appears on jewellery, tattoos, amulets, and corporate logos across the globe, usually as a generic sign of protection. In popular culture, Horus features in films, comics, and games as a falcon-headed warrior or sky-god. For modern Kemetics and Egyptian pagans, Horus remains a living deity of kingship, justice, and rightful authority. The name has also entered astronomy: the asteroid 1924 Horus reminds us that the distant one still watches from above.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Horus is the god of the long view. The falcon sees what the ground-dweller cannot; the king must see beyond his own reign. To call on Horus is to remember that authority is not merely power but rightfulness — the triumph of ma'at over isfet, of inheritance over usurpation, of the whole over the torn.

The myth of Horus and Set is not a simple story of good versus evil. In some periods Set was the protector of Re's bark; in others he was the murderer of Osiris. The conflict is structural: order and disorder are relatives, not strangers, and their contention is what keeps the world awake. Horus wins not because he is strongest but because he is legitimate. That is the Egyptian lesson: cosmic order is maintained not by force alone but by the recognition of rightful place. The restored eye is the image of that order — broken, then made whole, then worn as a pledge that wholeness can be recovered.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name ḥr is written with the falcon-on-perch hieroglyph (Gardiner G5), often used as a logogram for the god himself. The initial ḥ is a voiceless pharyngeal fricative; the final r is an alveolar liquid. Because Egyptian does not write vowels, the pronunciation has to be reconstructed from Coptic forms such as ϩⲱⲣ and from Greek Ὧρος. The meaning 'distant one' or 'one on high' is well attested.

lore.archaeology: The falcon-god Horus is attested from the earliest dynastic period: the Narmer Palette shows a falcon protecting the king, and the serekh with Horus-name became the oldest royal titulary. The temple of Horus at Edfu, built during the Ptolemaic period, preserves the longest surviving ancient Egyptian temple inscription, including the myth of Horus defeating Set. Falcon mummies and votive falcon coffins have been found at Saqqara, Abydos, and Hierakonpolis — the latter city being Horus's ancient cult center.
